kicker: Ember · Science · Test on Wed 18 Nov
title: Day 4: Contact forces
sub: Day 4 (Sat). Friction and drag, then squashing and stretching (Hooke’s Law). About 25 minutes.
skill: The Because Chain: cause → effect → consequence.
target: Forces questions reward the chain force → resultant force → what happens to the motion, and for springs, numbers with units (extension = new length − original length).

sections.sub: Contact forces act when two things touch.

blocks.html:
Friction acts between two solid surfaces sliding past each other. Even smooth-looking surfaces are rough close up, so they grip. Rougher surfaces → more friction.
Drag acts on something moving through a fluid: air resistance in air, water resistance in water. The object has to push the particles out of the way. Faster → more drag.
Reduce friction: use oil or grease (lubrication). Reduce drag: a smooth, pointed (streamlined) shape.
Resultant force zero (forces balanced) → the object is in equilibrium: it stays still, or keeps moving at a steady speed in the same direction.

blocks.q: A dolphin swims through the sea. Which force slows it down?
blocks.why: Moving through water = water resistance, a drag force. Friction is between two solid surfaces.

blocks.q: On which surface is friction greater?
blocks.why: Rough surfaces grip each other more.

blocks.q: A leaf falls at a steady speed. What does that tell you about the forces on it?
o: Its weight is bigger than air resistance
Air resistance equals its weight, so the resultant force is zero
There are no forces on it
blocks.why: Steady speed = equilibrium = balanced forces. The forces are still there; they just cancel out.

blocks.q: A cyclist tucks her arms in and crouches low. Why?
o: To make herself more streamlined, so there is less air resistance
To increase friction with the road
blocks.why: A more streamlined shape pushes fewer air particles out of the way, so the drag is smaller.

blocks.q: A car’s engine pushes it forward with 2000 N. Air resistance and friction add up to 1500 N backwards. What is the resultant force?
blocks.why: 2000 − 1500 = 500 N forwards, so the car speeds up.

traps.msg: They act in opposite directions, so subtract.

blocks.html:
Forces can change the shape of an object: deformation. Squashing = compression; stretching = tension.
Why the floor holds you up: a solid’s particles are joined by bonds. Your weight squashes the bonds a tiny bit, and they push back. That support force is the reaction force.
Extension = how much longer something gets = new length − original length.
Hooke’s Law: for a spring, if you double the force, the extension doubles. The force–extension graph is a straight line through the origin: a linear relationship (force and extension are proportional).
Past its elastic limit, a spring no longer goes back to its original length. Not everything obeys Hooke’s Law: an elastic band or a plastic bag (polyethene) does not.

blocks.q: Why don’t you fall through a chair when you sit on it?
o: The chair is heavier than you
Your weight slightly compresses the bonds between the chair’s particles, and they push back up with a reaction force
blocks.why: The chair deforms a tiny bit; the compressed bonds push back. That is the reaction (support) force.

blocks.q: A spring is 4 cm long. When a weight hangs on it, it is 7 cm long. What is the extension?

traps.msg: That is the new length. Extension = new length − original length.

blocks.q: A 2 N force stretches a spring by 3 cm. The spring obeys Hooke’s Law. What is the extension with a 6 N force?
blocks.why: 6 N is 3 × 2 N, so the extension is 3 × 3 cm = 9 cm.

traps.msg: The force tripled, so the extension triples: 9 cm.

blocks.q: What does a straight line through the origin on a force–extension graph show?
o: The spring has passed its elastic limit
Force and extension are proportional (a linear relationship), so the spring obeys Hooke’s Law
blocks.why: Straight line through (0,0) = proportional = Hooke’s Law.

blocks.q: A spring is stretched too far and stays longer when the force is removed. What has happened?
o: It has gone past its elastic limit
blocks.why: Past the elastic limit it is permanently stretched.

blocks.q: A skydiver jumps. Why does she stop speeding up? Tap the links in order.
items: As she falls faster, she hits more air particles each second.
So the air resistance on her increases.
Eventually air resistance equals her weight, so the resultant force is zero.
So she falls at a steady speed.
blocks.done: Faster → more drag → balanced forces → steady speed.

blocks.q: Explain why a car with smooth, worn tyres is more likely to skid on the road than a car with new tyres.

points.t: new tyres are rougher / have more grip
so there is more friction between the tyres and the road
worn (smooth) tyres give less friction, so the car slides more easily / takes longer to stop

blocks.q: A student hangs weights on a spring and a rubber band and plots force–extension graphs. Describe how the two graphs would be different, and what that tells you.

points.t: the spring’s graph is a straight line through the origin
so the spring obeys Hooke’s Law / extension is proportional to force
the rubber band’s graph is curved (not linear), so it does not obey Hooke’s Law

items: I can name friction, air resistance and water resistance, and say when each acts.
I can say how to reduce friction (lubrication) and drag (streamlining).
Balanced forces → still, or steady speed.
Hooke’s Law: double the force, double the extension; straight line through the origin.

blocks.q: “Why does the floor push up on you?”
blocks.note: For the parent: listen for weight compresses the bonds between particles, and they push back: the reaction force. “Because it’s solid” is not enough: ask “what happens to the particles?”
